Name: E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase HECTD3
ShortDescription: E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase HECTD3 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that regulates ubiquitination and degradation of Tara [[cite:PUB00071270]], MASTL and LKB1 [[cite:PUB00093000]]. HECTD3 interacts with HSP90 and is involved in the HSP90-dependent degradation of CRAF protein [[cite:PUB00093000]]. It has been shown to interact and stabilize MALT1 (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue 1), and may hence promote cell survival [[cite:PUB00093001]].

Name: Little elongation complex subunit 2 , C-terminal
ShortDescription: This entry represents the C-terminal of little elongation complex subunit 2 (ICE2, also known as NARG2). ICE2 is a component of the little elongation complex (LEC), a complex required to regulate small nuclear RNA (snRNA) gene transcription by RNA polymerase II and III [[cite:PUB00072917], [cite:PUB00072918]]. This C-terminal domain belongs to the PD-(D/E)XK nuclease superfamily [[cite:PUB00066699]].

Name: cAMP-responsive element-binding ATF subfamily
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes transcriptional activators that are involved in the unfolded protein response (UPR) and cellular stress responses. They bind to specific DNA elements such as the cAMP response element (CRE) and the unfolded protein response element (UPRE), thereby regulating gene expression. These proteins play roles in various cellular processes including cell survival, proliferation, migration, differentiation, and inflammatory responses. They are also implicated in the regulation of lipid metabolism, particularly in maintaining normal plasma triglyceride concentrations. Some family members are involved in the response to endoplasmic reticulum stress by activating target genes that help in adapting to and surviving stress conditions. Additionally, they may interact with other transcription factors and histone deacetylases to modulate transcriptional outcomes.

Name: Multidrug transporter EmrE superfamily
ShortDescription:
This superfamily, with a founding member EmrE, represents a number of membrane transporters some of which involved in multidrug resistance. Members contain four non-compact transmembrane helices that can oligomerise.

;

EmrE, a multidrug transporter from Escherichia coli, functions as a homodimer of a small four-transmembrane protein. It confers resistance to a wide range of toxic compounds, including ethidium, methyl viologen, acriflavine, tetraphenylphosphonium (TPP+), benzalkonium, propidium, dequalinium and the aminoglycoside antibiotics streptomycin and tobramycin [[cite:PUB00159766], [cite:PUB00160800], [cite:PUB00159767], [cite:PUB00050516], [cite:PUB00160801], [cite:PUB00160802]].

;

The Undecaprenyl phosphate-aminoarabinose (also known as 4-amino-4-deoxy-L-arabinose-phosphoundecaprenol) flippase subunit ArnE translocates 4-amino-4-deoxy-L-arabinose-phosphoundecaprenol from the cytoplasmic to the periplasmic side of the inner membrane and is involved in the lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis.

Name: Transmembrane protein 42
ShortDescription: The function of TMEM42 is not known.

Name: Bacterial exopeptidase dimerisation domain
ShortDescription: This superfamily consists of a protein domain with four β strands and two α helices which make up the dimerisation surface of members of the MEROPS peptidase family M20 [[cite:PUB00015203]]. This entry includes a range of zinc exopeptidases: carboxypeptidases, dipeptidases and specialised aminopeptidases [[cite:PUB00003579]].

Name: Peptidase M20, dimerisation domain
ShortDescription: This domain consists of 4 β-strands and two α-helices which make up the dimerisation surface of members of the MEROPS peptidase family M20 [[cite:PUB00015203]]. This family includes a range of zinc exopeptidases: carboxypeptidases, dipeptidases and specialised aminopeptidases [[cite:PUB00003579]].

Name: Peptidase M20A
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the MEROPS peptidase subfamily M20A (clan MH), which includes human N-fatty-acyl-amino acid synthase/hydrolase PM20D1, Carboxypeptidase S from Saccharomyces cerevisiae and similar eukaryotic and bacterial sequences. PM20D1 is a secreted enzyme that regulates the endogenous N-fatty acyl amino acid (NAAs) tissue and circulating levels by functioning as a bidirectional NAA synthase/hydrolase [[cite:PUB00102097]]. Carboxypeptidase S, which is used for certain peptides as sole nitrogen source, has a preference for releasing an amino acid attached to Gly [[cite:PUB00085108]]. The peptidases of this protein family have two catalytic zinc ions at the active site, bound by His/Asp, Asp, Glu, Asp/Glu and His. The catalysed reaction involves the release of an N-terminal amino acid, usually neutral or hydrophobic, from a polypeptide [[cite:PUB00003579]].

;

Over 70 metallopeptidase families have been identified to date. In these enzymes a divalent cation, which is usually zinc but may be cobalt, manganese or copper, activates the water molecule. The metal ion is held in place by amino acid ligands, usually three in number. In some families of co-catalytic metallopeptidases, two metal ions are observed in crystal structures ligated by five amino acids, with one amino acid ligating both metal ions. The known metal ligands are His, Glu, Asp or Lys. At least one other residue is required for catalysis, which may play an electrophilic role. Many metalloproteases contain an HEXXH motif, which has been shown in crystallographic studies to form part of the metal-binding site [[cite:PUB00003579]]. The HEXXH motif is relatively common but can be more stringently defined for metalloproteases as 'abXHEbbHbc', where 'a' is most often valine or threonine and forms part of the S1' subsite in thermolysin and neprilysin, 'b' is an uncharged residue, and 'c' a hydrophobic residue. Proline is never found in this site, possibly because it would break the helical structure adopted by this motif in metalloproteases [[cite:PUB00003579]].

Name: Peptidase M20
ShortDescription:
This group of proteins contains the metallopeptidases and non-peptidase homologues (amidohydrolases) that belong to the MEROPS peptidase family M20 (clan MH) [[cite:PUB00003579]]. The peptidases of this clan have two catalytic zinc ions at the active site, bound by His/Asp, Asp, Glu, Asp/Glu and His. The catalysed reaction involves the release of an N-terminal amino acid, usually neutral or hydrophobic, from a polypeptide [[cite:PUB00003579]]. The peptidase M20 family has four subfamilies:

  • M20A -type example, glutamate carboxypeptidase from Pseudomonas sp. RS16 ([swissprot:P06621])
  • M20B -type example, peptidase T from Escherichia coli ([swissprot:P29745])
  • M20C -type example, X-His dipeptidase from E. coli ([swissprot:P15288])
  • M20D -type example, carboxypeptidase Ss1 from Sulfolobus solfataricus ([swissprot:P80092])

Homologues from the family that are not peptidases include:

  • Acetylornithine deacetylase, which releases an acetyl group and L-ornithine from N(2)-acetyl-L-ornithine [[cite:PUB00014890]]
  • N-acetyldiaminopimelate deacetylase, which catalyses the conversion of N-acetyl-diaminopimelate to diaminopimelate and acetate [[cite:PUB00085192]]
  • N-carbamoyl-L-amino-acid hydrolase, which converts D,L-5-monosubstituted hydantoins into D-or L-amino acids [[cite:PUB00019732]]
  • Aminoacylase-1, which hydrolyses N-acylated or N-acetylated amino acids [[cite:PUB00030157]]
  • Succinyl-diaminopimelate desuccinylase ([ec:3.5.1.18]), which catalyses the hydrolysis of N-succinyl-L,L-diaminopimelic acid, forming succinate and LL-2,6-diaminoheptanedioate (DAP, a component of bacterial cell walls) [[cite:PUB00079915]]

Name: Type-1 angiotensin II receptor-associated protein
ShortDescription: AGTRAP (type-1 angiotensin II receptor-associated protein) appears to be a negative regulator of type-1 angiotensin II receptor-mediated signalling by regulating receptor internalisation as well as mechanism of receptor desensitization such as phosphorylation [[cite:PUB00019116]]. It plays an important role in cardiac hypertrophy [[cite:PUB00078888]].

Name: SAS-6, N-terminal domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
Spindle assembly abnormal protein 6 (SAS-6) is the centre of the cartwheel assembly that scaffolds centrioles early in their biogenesis. Structural studies have shown that SAS-6 self-associates in vitro into assemblies that resemble cartwheel centres through the formation of a parallel coiled-coil dimer [[cite:PUB00056547]].

This entry represents the N-terminal domain of the SAS-6 , both in C.elegans and in humans. The N-terminal domain is the region through which the 9 rod-shaped homodimers that SAS-6 forms on oligomerisation interact with each other. Proper functioning of the centriole requires this correct oligomerisation [[cite:PUB00058831]].

Name: SAS-6 coiled-coil domain
ShortDescription: This is a coiled-coil domain found at the C terminus of spindle assembly abnormal protein 6 (Sas6). The highly conserved protein SAS-6 constitutes the centre of the cartwheel assembly that scaffolds centrioles early in their biogenesis. Structural analysis of Sas6 show that similar to XLF and XRCC4, it forms a parallel coiled-coil dimer [[cite:PUB00056547]].

Name: EGF-like calcium-binding domain
ShortDescription:
A sequence of about forty amino-acid residues found in epidermal growth factor (EGF) has been shown [[cite:PUB00004321], [cite:PUB00004609], [cite:PUB00004964], [cite:PUB00003983], [cite:PUB00001555]] to be present in a large number of membrane-bound and extracellular, mostly animal, proteins. Many of these proteins require calcium for their biological function, and a calcium-binding site has been found at the N-terminal of some EGF-like domains [[cite:PUB00002741]]. Calcium-binding may be crucial for numerous protein-protein interactions.

A common feature of all EGF-like domains is that they are found in the extracellular domain of membrane-bound proteins or in proteins known to be secreted (exception: prostaglandin G/H synthase). The EGF-like domain includes six cysteine residues which have been shown to be involved in disulfide bonds. The structure of several EGF-like domains has been solved. The fold consists of two-stranded β-sheet followed by a loop to a C-terminal short two-stranded sheet.

As in non-calcium binding EGF-like domains, there are six conserved cysteines and the structure of both types is very similar as calcium-binding induces only strictly local structural changes [[cite:PUB00002741]].

                             +------------------+        +---------+
                             |                  |        |         |
               nxnnC-x(3,14)-C-x(3,7)-CxxbxxxxaxC-x(1,6)-C-x(8,13)-Cx
                   |                  | 
                   +------------------+

'n': negatively charged or polar residue [DEQN]
'b': possibly beta-hydroxylated residue [DN]
'a': aromatic amino acid
'C': cysteine, involved in disulphide bond
'x': any amino acid.

Name: EGF-type aspartate/asparagine hydroxylation site
ShortDescription: Post-translational hydroxylation of aspartic acid or asparagine [[cite:PUB00002475]] to form erythro-beta-hydroxyaspartic acid or erythro-beta-hydroxyasparagine has been identified in a number of proteins with domains homologous to epidermal growth factor (EGF). Examples of such proteins are the blood coagulation protein factors VII, IX and X, proteins C, S, and Z, the LDL receptor, thrombomodulin, etc. Based on sequence comparisons of the EGF-homology region that contains hydroxylated Asp or Asn, a consensus sequence has been identified that seems to be required by the hydroxylase(s).

Name: GRB10-interacting GYF
ShortDescription: The GIGYF family proteins are involved in the regulation of translation initiation and mRNA decay. They are key components of the 4EHP-GYF2 complex, which represses translation initiation by sequestering the mRNA cap, thus blocking ribosome initiation and reducing the translational load on problematic messages. This complex also links translation repression with mRNA decay by recruiting decapping effector proteins and the deadenylation CCR4-NOT complex. GIGYF proteins may cooperate with GRB10 to modulate tyrosine kinase receptor signaling, including IGF1 and insulin receptors. They are implicated in ribosome-associated quality control (RQC) by sequestering faulty mRNA, working downstream of ZNF598. Additionally, GIGYF proteins are involved in cellular responses to stress, such as starvation-induced autophagy, and play a role in maintaining tissue homeostasis. In the context of viral infection, GIGYF proteins can affect the translation of genes involved in the antiviral immune response.

Name: GYF domain
ShortDescription:
The glycine-tyrosine-phenylalanine (GYF) domain is an around 60-amino acid domain which contains a conserved GP[YF]xxxx[MV]xxWxxx[GN]YF motif. It was identified in the human intracellular protein termed CD2 binding protein 2 (CD2BP2), which binds to a site containing two tandem PPPGHR segments within the cytoplasmic region of CD2. Binding experiments and mutational analyses have demonstrated the critical importance of the GYF tripeptide in ligand binding. A GYF domain is also found in several other eukaryotic proteins of unknown function [[cite:PUB00011823]]. It has been proposed that the GYF domain found in these proteins could also be involved in proline-rich sequence recognition [[cite:PUB00011824]].

Resolution of the structure of the CD2BP2 GYF domain by NMR spectroscopy revealed a compact domain with a β-β-α-β-β topology, where the single α-helix is tilted away from the twisted, anti-parallel β-sheet. The conserved residues of the GYF domain create a contiguous patch of predominantly hydrophobic nature which forms an integral part of the ligand-binding site [[cite:PUB00011824]]. There is limited homology within the C-terminal 20-30 amino acids of various GYF domains, supporting the idea that this part of the domain is structurally but not functionally important [[cite:PUB00011825]].

This entry also matches Arabidopsis histone methyltransferases ATXR3/SDG2 and ATXR7/SDG25, which contain two partial GYF domains towards the N terminus [[cite:PUB00085701]]. Histone methyltransferase ATXR7 is involved in regulation of flowering time [[cite:PUB00085379]]. It is specifically required for the trimethylation of 'Lys-4' of histone H3 (H3K4me3) at the FLC locus, it prevents the trimethylation on 'Lys-27' (H3K27me3) at the same locus. ATXR3 is also required for H3K4 trimethylation and is crucial for both sporophyte and gametophyte development in plants [[cite:PUB00085380], [cite:PUB00085381]].

Name: F-box associated (FBA) domain
ShortDescription: F-box proteins have a bipartite structure: they contain a carboxy-terminal domain that interacts with substrates and a 42-48 amino-acid F-box domain which binds to the protein Skp1. A subset of F-box proteins is characterised by a ~180-residue carboxy-terminal region, which has been called the F-box-associated (FBA) domain [[cite:PUB00009973], [cite:PUB00018546]]. A FBA domain has also been identified in the catfish, tilapia, and zebrafish nonspecific cytotoxic cell receptor proteins (NCCRP-1), which do not contain the F-box domain. NCCRP-1 may function as an antigen recognition molecule and, as such, may participate in innate immunity in teleosts [[cite:PUB00018546], [cite:PUB00018547]]. The FBA domain is likely to be a glycoprotein-binding module [[cite:PUB00018548], [cite:PUB00018549]].

Name: F-box only protein
ShortDescription: Proteins in this entry contain an N-terminal F-box and a C-terminal F-box associated (FBA) domain. The F-box is a conserved domain that is present in numerous proteins with a bipartite structure [[cite:PUB00000938]]. Through the F-box, these proteins are linked to the Skp1 protein and the core of SCFs (Skp1-cullin-F-box protein ligase) complexes. SCFs complexes constitute a new class of E3 ligases [[cite:PUB00000952]]. They function in combination with the E2 enzyme Cdc34 to ubiquitinate G1 cyclins, Cdk inhibitors and many other proteins, to mark them for degradation. The binding of the specific substrates by SCFs complexes is mediated by divergent protein-protein interaction motifs present in F-box proteins, like WD40 repeats, leucine rich repeats [[cite:PUB00018180], [cite:PUB00018181]] or ANK repeats.

Name: Large ribosomal subunit protein uL29 superfamily
ShortDescription:
This family includes ribosomal proteins, which constitute the uL29 family [[cite:PUB00080279]]. These were previously known as L29 from eubacteria and archaea and L35 from eukaryotes.

;

Ribosomal protein uL29 is one of the proteins from the large ribosomal subunit. uL29 belongs to a family of ribosomal proteins of 63 to 138 amino-acid residues which, on the basis of sequence similarities, groups:

  • Red algal uL29.
  • Bacterial uL29.
  • Mammalian uL29 (known as L35)
  • Caenorhabditis elegans uL29 (known as L35) (ZK652.4).
  • Yeast uL29 (known as L35).

uL29 is located on the surface of the large ribosomal subunit, where it participates in forming a protein ring that surrounds the polypeptide exit channel, providing structural support for the ribosome [[cite:PUB00079483]]. uL29 is involved in forming the translocon binding site, along with L19, L22, L23, L24, and L31e. In addition, uL29 and L23 form the interaction site for trigger factor (TF) on the ribosomal surface, adjacent to the exit tunnel [[cite:PUB00080476]]. uL29 forms numerous interactions with L23 and with the 23S rRNA.

;

Ribosomes are the particles that catalyse mRNA-directed protein synthesis in all organisms. The codons of the mRNA are exposed on the ribosome to allow tRNA binding. This leads to the incorporation of amino acids into the growing polypeptide chain in accordance with the genetic information. Incoming amino acid monomers enter the ribosomal A site in the form of aminoacyl-tRNAs complexed with elongation factor Tu (EF-Tu) and GTP. The growing polypeptide chain, situated in the P site as peptidyl-tRNA, is then transferred to aminoacyl-tRNA, and the new peptidyl-tRNA, extended by one residue, is translocated to the P site with the aid of the elongation factor G (EF-G) and GTP as the deacylated tRNA is released from the ribosome through one or more exit sites [[cite:PUB00007068], [cite:PUB00007069]]. About 2/3 of the mass of the ribosome consists of RNA and 1/3 consists of protein. The proteins are named in accordance with the subunit of the ribosome which they belong to: the small (S1 to S31) and the large (L1 to L44). Usually they decorate the rRNA cores of the subunits.

Many ribosomal proteins, particularly those of the large subunit, are composed of a globular, surfaced-exposed domain with long finger-like projections that extend into the rRNA core to stabilise its structure. Most of the proteins interact with multiple RNA elements, often from different domains. In the large subunit, about 1/3 of the 23S rRNA nucleotides are at least in van der Waals' contact with protein, and L22 interacts with all six domains of the 23S rRNA. Proteins S4 and S7, which initiate assembly of the 16S rRNA, are located at junctions of five and four RNA helices, respectively. In this way, proteins serve to organise and stabilise the rRNA tertiary structure. While the crucial activities of decoding and peptide transfer are RNA-based, proteins play an active role in functions that may have evolved to streamline the process of protein synthesis. In addition to their function in the ribosome, many ribosomal proteins have some function 'outside' the ribosome [[cite:PUB00007069], [cite:PUB00007070]].

Name: 2-C-methyl-D-erythritol 2,4-cyclodiphosphate synthase superfamily
ShortDescription:
IspF is a MECDP (2-C-methyl-D-erythritol 2,4-cyclodiphosphate) synthetase, also known as YgbB. It is an enzyme in the non-mevalonate pathway of isoprenoid synthesis. Isoprenoids are essential in all organisms, and can also be synthesized through the mevalonate pathway. The non-mevolante route is used by many bacteria and human pathogens, including Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Plasmodium falciparum. This route appears to involve seven enzymes. MECDP synthetase catalyses the intramolecular attack by a phosphate group on a diphosphate, with cytidine monophosphate (CMP) acting as the leaving group to give the cyclic diphosphate product MEDCP. The enzyme is a trimer with three active sites shared between adjacent copies of the protein. The enzyme also has two metal binding sites, the metals playing key roles in catalysis[[cite:PUB00021869]].

A number of proteins from eukaryotes and prokaryotes are bifunctional proteins with an N-terminal IspD domain and a C-terminal IspF domain [[cite:PUB00056865]].

;

Structurally, IpsF forms trimers with three closely packed β-sheets.

Name: Cytidylyltransferase IspD/TarI
ShortDescription:
This family consists of cytidylyltransferases IspD and TarI and close homologues.

;

This mevalonate independent pathway that utilizes pyruvate and glyceraldehydes 3-phosphate as starting materials for production of IPP occurs in a variety of bacteria, archaea and plant cells, but is absent in mammals. The isoprenoid pathway is a well known target for anti-infective drug development [[cite:PUB00043297], [cite:PUB00043298]]. In about twenty percent of bacterial genomes, this protein occurs as IspDF, a bifunctional fusion protein.

;

Ribitol-5-phosphate cytidylyltransferase (TarI) is required for the synthesis of activated ribitol via the wall teichoic acid biosynthesis pathway. The enzyme catalyzes the transfer of the cytidylyl group of CTP to D-ribitol 5-phosphate to form CDP-ribitol [[cite:PUB00049880]].

It is implicated in dystroglycan O-mannosylation [[cite:PUB00084173], [cite:PUB00084174]].

D-fructose-6-phosphate cytidylyltransferase catalyses the formation of CDP-6-d-fructose from cytidine triphosphate and d-fructose-6-phosphate and is involved in the biosynthesis of capsular polysaccharides [[cite:PUB00154498]]. It could also utilise other sugar donors such as D-fructose-1-phosphate, D-glucose-6-phosphate, alpha-D-glucose-1-phosphate or D-glucitol-6-phosphate [[cite:PUB00154498]].

Name: L-Aspartase-like
ShortDescription: The enzyme L-aspartate ammonia-lyase (aspartase) catalyses the reversible deamination of the amino acid L-aspartic acid via a carbanion mechanism, producing fumaric acid and an ammonium ion. ShortDescription:
This superfamily represents the EC2 domain from tetraspanins, consisting of 5 helices in an irregular disulphide-linked array which plays a role in form homodimerization.

Tetraspanins are a distinct family of cell surface proteins, containing four conserved transmembrane domains: a small outer loop (EC1), a larger outer loop (EC2), a small inner loop (IL) and short cytoplasmic tails. They contain characteristic structural features, including 4-6 conserved extracellular cysteine residues, and polar residues within transmembrane domains.

A fundamental role of tetraspanins appears to be organising other proteins into a network of multimolecular membrane microdomains, sometimes called the 'tetraspanin web'. Within this web there are primary complexes in which tetraspanins show robust, specific, and direct lateral associations with other proteins. The strong tendency of tetraspanins to associate with each other probably contributes to the assembly of a network of secondary interactions in which non-tetraspanin proteins are associated with each other via palmitoylated tetraspanins acting as linker proteins. In addition, the association of lipids, such as gangliosides and cholesterol, probably contributes to the assembly of even larger tetraspanin complexes, which have some lipid raft-like properties (e.g. resistance to solubilization in non-ionic detergents). Within the tetraspanin web, tetraspanin proteins can associate not only with integrins and other transmembrane proteins, but also with signalling enzymes such as protein kinase C and phosphatidylinositol-4 kinase. Thus, the tetraspanin web provides a mechanistic framework by which membrane protein signalling can be expanded into a lateral dimension [[cite:PUB00010633]].

Name: Leucine-rich repeat, typical subtype
ShortDescription:
Leucine-rich repeats (LRR) consist of 2-45 motifs of 20-30 amino acids in length that generally folds into an arc or horseshoe shape [[cite:PUB00017058]]. LRRs occur in proteins ranging from viruses to eukaryotes, and appear to provide a structural framework for the formation of protein-protein interactions [[cite:PUB00007147], [cite:PUB00001625]].Proteins containing LRRs include tyrosine kinase receptors, cell-adhesion molecules, virulence factors, and extracellular matrix-binding glycoproteins, and are involved in a variety of biological processes, including signal transduction, cell adhesion, DNA repair, recombination, transcription, RNA processing, disease resistance, apoptosis, and the immune response [[cite:PUB00001898], [cite:PUB00094376]].

Sequence analyses of LRR proteins suggested the existence of several different subfamilies of LRRs. The significance of this classification is that repeats from different subfamilies never occur simultaneously and have most probably evolved independently. It is, however, now clear that all major classes of LRR have curved horseshoe structures with a parallel β sheet on the concave side and mostly helical elements on the convex side. At least six families of LRR proteins, characterised by different lengths and consensus sequences of the repeats, have been identified. Eleven-residue segments of the LRRs (LxxLxLxxN/CxL), corresponding to the β-strand and adjacent loop regions, are conserved in LRR proteins, whereas the remaining parts of the repeats (herein termed variable) may be very different. Despite the differences, each of the variable parts contains two half-turns at both ends and a "linear" segment (as the chain follows a linear path overall), usually formed by a helix, in the middle. The concave face and the adjacent loops are the most common protein interaction surfaces on LRR proteins. 3D structure of some LRR proteins-ligand complexes show that the concave surface of LRR domain is ideal for interaction with α-helix, thus supporting earlier conclusions that the elongated and curved LRR structure provides an outstanding framework for achieving diverse protein-protein interactions [[cite:PUB00007147]]. Molecular modeling suggests that the conserved pattern LxxLxL, which is shorter than the previously proposed LxxLxLxxN/CxL is sufficient to impart the characteristic horseshoe curvature to proteins with 20-to 30-residue repeats [[cite:PUB00007148]].

Name: Leucine-rich repeat and transmembrane domain-containing protein
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes a variety of members with diverse functions, primarily involved in cellular signaling, synaptic adhesion, and regulation of neuronal activity. Some act as inhibitors, such as those that inhibit TGF-beta signaling or phospholipase A2 activity. Others are involved in the immune response, bone homeostasis, and regulation of the JAK/STAT pathway. Notably, several members function as receptors that mediate axonal growth inhibition and neuronal plasticity, interacting with ligands like RTN4, OMG, and MAG, and are implicated in brain development and synaptic organization. Additionally, some proteins in this family are involved in the negative regulation of viral infection and in the formation of platelet plugs.

Name: Chemokine-like protein TAFA
ShortDescription: This family is composed of five highly homologous small secreted proteins, TAFA1-5. These proteins contain conserved cysteine residues at fixed positions, and are distantly related to MIP-1alpha, a member of the CC-chemokine family. The FAM19/TAFA proteins are predominantly expressed in specific regions of the brain, and are postulated to function as brain-specific chemokines or neurokines that act as regulators of immune and nervous cells [[cite:PUB00045989]]. Mouse TAFA2 is involved in neuronal survival and neurobiological functions [[cite:PUB00092771]]. TAFA5 has been shown to inhibit postinjury neointima formation via sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor 2-G12/13-RhoA signaling [[cite:PUB00090824]].

Name: TAFA chemokine-like
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes chemokine-like factors that are involved in various biological processes related to the immune system and neuronal functions. Members of this family have been shown to play roles in modulating pain hypersensitivity, chemoattracting macrophages, promoting phagocytosis, and increasing reactive oxygen species release. They are also implicated in the regulation of microglia polarization and act as neurotrophic factors contributing to neuronal survival and neurobiological functions. Additionally, some proteins in this family serve as ligands for specific receptors, influencing neural stem-cell proliferation and differentiation.

Name: Ras-specific palmitoyltransferase complex
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes palmitoyltransferases that are involved in the post-translational modification of Ras proteins, which is crucial for their proper localization to the plasma membrane and subsequent function in cell signaling. Members of this family form complexes, such as ERF2-ERF4 in yeast and ZDHHC9-GOLGA7 in mammals, which specifically palmitoylate Ras proteins like RAS2, HRAS, and NRAS. This modification is essential for the anchoring of these Ras proteins to the plasma membrane, where they participate in signal transduction pathways that regulate cell growth and differentiation. Some family members are also implicated in protein transport from the Golgi apparatus to the cell surface and may play roles in cell adhesion.

Name: Golgin subfamily A member 7/ERF4
ShortDescription: Proteins in this entry include Golgin subfamily A member 7 and the Ras modification protein ERF4.

Name: IL-40-like, Ig domain
ShortDescription: This Ig domain is found in tandem in IL-40 (also known as C17orf99), which is found across mammalian species [[cite:PUB00103720]]. It is a B cell-associated cytokine that plays important roles in humoral immune responses and may also play a role in B cell development. It is expressed in bone marrow and fetal liver and its expression is also induced in peripheral B cells upon activation [[cite:PUB00103720]]. This domain is also found in many proteins from animals, apart from mammals.

Name: Large ribosomal subunit protein uL10, bacteria/organella
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the large ribosomal subunit protein uL10 family found in bacteria and in eukaryotic organelles such as mitochondria and chloroplast.

;

Ribosomes are the particles that catalyse mRNA-directed protein synthesis in all organisms. The codons of the mRNA are exposed on the ribosome to allow tRNA binding. This leads to the incorporation of amino acids into the growing polypeptide chain in accordance with the genetic information. Incoming amino acid monomers enter the ribosomal A site in the form of aminoacyl-tRNAs complexed with elongation factor Tu (EF-Tu) and GTP. The growing polypeptide chain, situated in the P site as peptidyl-tRNA, is then transferred to aminoacyl-tRNA, and the new peptidyl-tRNA, extended by one residue, is translocated to the P site with the aid of the elongation factor G (EF-G) and GTP as the deacylated tRNA is released from the ribosome through one or more exit sites [[cite:PUB00007068], [cite:PUB00007069]]. About 2/3 of the mass of the ribosome consists of RNA and 1/3 consists of protein. The proteins are named in accordance with the subunit of the ribosome which they belong to: the small (S1 to S31) and the large (L1 to L44). Usually they decorate the rRNA cores of the subunits.

Many ribosomal proteins, particularly those of the large subunit, are composed of a globular, surfaced-exposed domain with long finger-like projections that extend into the rRNA core to stabilise its structure. Most of the proteins interact with multiple RNA elements, often from different domains. In the large subunit, about 1/3 of the 23S rRNA nucleotides are at least in van der Waals' contact with protein, and L22 interacts with all six domains of the 23S rRNA. Proteins S4 and S7, which initiate assembly of the 16S rRNA, are located at junctions of five and four RNA helices, respectively. In this way, proteins serve to organise and stabilise the rRNA tertiary structure. While the crucial activities of decoding and peptide transfer are RNA-based, proteins play an active role in functions that may have evolved to streamline the process of protein synthesis. In addition to their function in the ribosome, many ribosomal proteins have some function 'outside' the ribosome [[cite:PUB00007069], [cite:PUB00007070]].

Name: Armadillo
ShortDescription:
This entry represents proteins that contain the Armadillo repeat mainly from eukaryotes. These proteins include: Vacuolar protein 8, Importins, Catenins, Junction plakoglobin and related proteins.

;

The armadillo (Arm) repeat is an approximately 40 amino acid long tandemly repeated sequence motif first identified in the Drosophila melanogaster segment polarity gene armadillo involved in signal transduction through wingless. Animal Arm-repeat proteins function in various processes, including intracellular signalling and cytoskeletal regulation, and include such proteins as beta-catenin, the junctional plaque protein plakoglobin, the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) tumour suppressor protein, and the nuclear transport factor importin-alpha, amongst others [[cite:PUB00015440]]. A subset of these proteins is conserved across eukaryotic kingdoms. In higher plants, some Arm-repeat proteins function in intracellular signalling like their mammalian counterparts, while others have novel functions [[cite:PUB00015441]]. The 3-dimensional fold of an armadillo repeat is known from the crystal structure of beta-catenin, where the 12 repeats form a superhelix of α helices with three helices per unit [[cite:PUB00000951]]. The cylindrical structure features a positively charged grove, which presumably interacts with the acidic surfaces of the known interaction partners of beta-catenin.

Name: Paraneoplastic antigen-like protein 8A, C-terminal
ShortDescription: This entry represents a conserved helical region found at the C-terminal of paraneoplastic antigen-like protein 8A (PNM8A), a protein whose function is still unknown.

Name: Paraneoplastic antigen Ma
ShortDescription:
The paraneoplastic Ma antigens (PNMA) have been identified using sera from patients with paraneoplastic neurological syndromes [[cite:PUB00060559]]. This entry includes paraneoplastic antigen PNMA1 [[cite:PUB00060560]], PNMA2 [[cite:PUB00060561]], PNMA3 [[cite:PUB00060562]], PNMA4 (also known as modulator of apoptosis 1 or MOAP-1) [[cite:PUB00060563]] and some paraneoplastic antigen-like proteins (PNMA5 and PNMA6). PNMA4/MOAP-1 has a role in death receptor-dependent apoptosis [[cite:PUB00069902]], and it also plays a role in autophagy as it promotes phagophore closure via association with ATG8 proteins [[cite:PUB00151898]].

Zinc finger CCHC domain-containing protein 12 (ZCCHC12, also known as Sizn1 in mouse), also a member of this entry, is a transcriptional coactivator in the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP)-signaling pathway. It positively modulates BMP signaling by interacting with SMAD1 and associating with CBP in the transcription complex. It contributes to the BMP-induced enhancement of cholinergic-neuron-specific gene expression [[cite:PUB00151899]]. This protein may be a potential molecular marker of papillary thyroid carcinoma [[cite:PUB00151900]].

Name: Paraneoplastic antigen Ma-like, N-terminal domain
ShortDescription:
This domain resembles an RNA-binding RRM domain in AlphaFold structure predictions. This domain is found at the N-terminal of various of paraneoplastic Ma antigens (PNMA) and similar proteins.

;

The paraneoplastic Ma antigens (PNMA) have been identified using sera from patients with paraneoplastic neurological syndromes [[cite:PUB00060559]]. This entry includes paraneoplastic antigen PNMA1 [[cite:PUB00060560]], PNMA2 [[cite:PUB00060561]], PNMA3 [[cite:PUB00060562]], PNMA4 (also known as modulator of apoptosis 1 or MOAP-1) [[cite:PUB00060563]] and some paraneoplastic antigen-like proteins (PNMA5 and PNMA6). PNMA4/MOAP-1 has a role in death receptor-dependent apoptosis [[cite:PUB00069902]], and it also plays a role in autophagy as it promotes phagophore closure via association with ATG8 proteins [[cite:PUB00151898]].

Zinc finger CCHC domain-containing protein 12 (ZCCHC12, also known as Sizn1 in mouse), also a member of this entry, is a transcriptional coactivator in the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP)-signaling pathway. It positively modulates BMP signaling by interacting with SMAD1 and associating with CBP in the transcription complex. It contributes to the BMP-induced enhancement of cholinergic-neuron-specific gene expression [[cite:PUB00151899]]. This protein may be a potential molecular marker of papillary thyroid carcinoma [[cite:PUB00151900]].

Name: Cullin-associated NEDD8-dissociated protein 1/2
ShortDescription: This entry includes cullin-associated NEDD8-dissociated proteins 1 (CAND1 also known as TIP120A) and 2 (CAND2); these proteins have a C-terminal TATA-binding protein interacting (TIP20) domain. CAND1 is required for the assembly of the SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase complex. The SCF ubiquitin E3 ligase consists of SKP1, CUL1 and F-box protein, and it regulates ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis. CAND1 binds to CUL1, preventing it from associating with the other components that form the ligase. Neddylation of CUL1 (or the presence of SKP1 and ATP) dissociates it from CAND1, allowing the ligase complex to form [[cite:PUB00090221], [cite:PUB00090222], [cite:PUB00090223]]. CAND1 also interacts with CUL3, a component of the Cul3-dependent E3 ubiquitin ligase complex [[cite:PUB00090224]]. CAND1 has been proposed to be an F-box protein exchange factor, and as substrates of the ligase complex are degraded by the proteasome and depleted, the ligase complex enters an intermediate, deneddylated state when CAND1 can bind, promoting dissociation of the substrate-recognition subunit and recruitment of a new substrate-recognition subunit [[cite:PUB00090225]]. CAND2 is uncharacterised but is assumed to have similar roles to CAND1.

Name: TATA-binding protein interacting (TIP20)
ShortDescription: TIP120 (also known as cullin-associated and neddylation-dissociated protein 1) is a TATA binding protein interacting protein that enhances transcription [[cite:PUB00033334]].

Name: Osteopetrosis-associated transmembrane protein 1 precursor
ShortDescription: Osteopetrosis-associated transmembrane protein 1 (OSTM1) is required for osteoclast and melanocyte maturation and function. Mutations in OSTM1 give rise to autosomal recessive osteopetrosis, also called autosomal recessive Albers-Schonberg disease [[cite:PUB00045058], [cite:PUB00045279]].

Name: V-set and immunoglobulin domain-containing protein 1
ShortDescription: V-set and immunoglobulin domain-containing protein 1 (VSIG1, also konwn as A34) belongs to the immunoglobulin superfamily (IgSF), whose members have one or more Ig-like domains in the extracellular region that is implicated in cell-cell adhesion, a transmembrane domain, and one cytoplasmic C-terminal region [[cite:PUB00071176]]. VSIG1 is required for the proper differentiation of glandular gastric epithelia [[cite:PUB00071176]].

Name: C1-like domain superfamily
ShortDescription: This superfamily includes variations of the protein kinase C1 domain that is characterised by a rich cysteine and histidine content. The C1 domain is the N-terminal region of conservation found in protein kinase C domains. This domain is involved in binding many ligands, which include diacylglycerol, phorbol esters and zinc [[cite:PUB00001427]]. This superfamily also includes the C-terminal domain of General transcription factor IIH subunit 2 whose structure revealed homology with the regulatory domain of protein kinase C [[cite:PUB00016526]].

Name: Serine/threonine-protein kinase
ShortDescription: The protein family is involved in a wide range of cellular processes, including signal transduction, cell cycle regulation, apoptosis, and immune responses. Members of this family are serine/threonine-protein kinases that act as regulatory links between membrane-associated GTPases and downstream MAPK cascades, determining cell fate decisions such as proliferation, differentiation, and survival. Some family members also have roles in stress responses, apoptosis, and necroptosis, acting as sensors or effectors in these pathways. They are involved in the phosphorylation of various substrates, including MAP kinase kinases, integrins, and histones, influencing pathways like JNK signaling, integrin-mediated signal transduction, and inflammatory responses. The family includes both catalytically active kinases and predicted pseudokinases with regulatory functions.

Name: Protein kinase C-like, phorbol ester/diacylglycerol-binding domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the N-terminal region of PKC, known as C1. It has been shown to bind PE and DAG in a phospholipid and zinc-dependent fashion [[cite:PUB00004685]]. The C1 region contains one or two copies (depending on the isozyme of PKC) of a cysteine-rich domain, which is about 50 amino-acid residues long, and which is essential for DAG/PE-binding. The DAG/PE-binding domain binds two zinc ions; the ligands of these metal ions are probably the six cysteines and two histidines that are conserved in this domain.

;

Protein kinase C (PKC) is a family of serine/threonine protein kinases found in eukaryotic organisms, including humans, animals, and fungi. These enzymes play crucial roles in various signal transduction cascades, regulating cellular processes such as gene expression, protein secretion, cell proliferation, and inflammatory responses [[cite:PUB00160329]]. PKCs are activated by second messengers, primarily diacylglycerol (DAG) [[cite:PUB00001427]]. The PKC family comprises multiple isozymes, categorised into three subfamilies: conventional, novel, and atypical, based on their second messenger requirements [[cite:PUB00119042]]. Structurally, PKCs consist of a regulatory domain and a catalytic domain connected by a hinge region [[cite:PUB00160328]]. The regulatory domain typically contains C1 [interpro:IPR002219] and C2 domain, which are responsible for DAG and calcium binding. The catalytic domain [interpro:IPR000719], highly conserved among PKC isozymes, contains the ATP- and substrate-binding sites.

Name: Kinase suppressor RAS 1, N-terminal helical hairpin
ShortDescription: Pseudokinases kinase suppressor of Ras 1 and 2 (KSR1/2) are scaffolds that bridge RAF isoforms and their substrate, mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MEK). They dimerize with kinase-competent RAFs (ARAF, BRAF and CRAF) to stimulate catalysis allosterically [[cite:PUB00101264]]. This entry represents the N-terminal helical hairpin which, together with the SAM-like domain ([InterPro:IPR025561]) constitutes the N-terminal regulatory region that mediates heterodimerization of BRAF with KSR1. Additionally, MEK binding to the kinase domain of KSR1 asymmetrically drives BRAF-KSR1 heterodimerization, resulting in the concomitant stimulation of BRAF catalytic activity towards free MEK molecules [[cite:PUB00101264]].

Name: Serine-threonine/tyrosine-protein kinase, catalytic domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the catalytic domain found in a number of serine/threonine- and tyrosine-protein kinases. It does not include catalytic domain of dual specificity kinases.

;

Protein phosphorylation, which plays a key role in most cellular activities, is a reversible process mediated by protein kinases and phosphoprotein phosphatases. Protein kinases catalyse the transfer of the gamma phosphate from nucleotide triphosphates (often ATP) to one or more amino acid residues in a protein substrate side chain, resulting in a conformational change affecting protein function. Phosphoprotein phosphatases catalyse the reverse process. Protein kinases fall into three broad classes, characterised with respect to substrate specificity [[cite:PUB00005115]]:

  • Serine/threonine-protein kinases
  • Tyrosine-protein kinases
  • Dual specificity protein kinases (e.g. MEK -phosphorylates both Thr and Tyr on target proteins)

Protein kinase function is evolutionarily conserved from Escherichia coli to human [[cite:PUB00020114]]. Protein kinases play a role in a multitude of cellular processes, including division, proliferation, apoptosis, and differentiation [[cite:PUB00015362]]. Phosphorylation usually results in a functional change of the target protein by changing enzyme activity, cellular location, or association with other proteins. The catalytic subunits of protein kinases are highly conserved, and several structures have been solved [[cite:PUB00034898]], leading to large screens to develop kinase-specific inhibitors for the treatments of a number of diseases [[cite:PUB00034899]].

Name: Kinase suppressor RAS 1, N-terminal helical hairpin superfamily
ShortDescription: Pseudokinases kinase suppressor of Ras 1 and 2 (KSR1/2) are scaffolds that bridge RAF isoforms and their substrate, mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MEK). They dimerize with kinase-competent RAFs (ARAF, BRAF and CRAF) to stimulate catalysis allosterically [[cite:PUB00101264]]. This entry represents the N-terminal helical hairpin which, together with the SAM-like domain ([InterPro:IPR025561]) constitutes the N-terminal regulatory region that mediates heterodimerization of BRAF with KSR1. Additionally, MEK binding to the kinase domain of KSR1 asymmetrically drives BRAF-KSR1 heterodimerization, resulting in the concomitant stimulation of BRAF catalytic activity towards free MEK molecules [[cite:PUB00101264]].

Name: E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase UBR1, UBR-box
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the UBR-box of human UBR1 and similar proteins found in vertebrates [[cite:PUB00103365]].

;

E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase UBR1 ([ec:2.3.2.27]), also called ubiquitin-protein ligase E3-alpha-I (E3alpha-I), or N-recognin-1, is a RING-type E3 ubiquitin ligase of the Arg/N-end rule degradation pathway. It recognises and binds to proteins bearing specific N-terminal residues that are destabilising according to the N-end rule, leading to their ubiquitination and subsequent degradation [[cite:PUB00103357], [cite:PUB00103353], [cite:PUB00058740], [cite:PUB00103354], [cite:PUB00103355], [cite:PUB00103352], [cite:PUB00103351], [cite:PUB00103356]]. Deficiency of UBR1 causes Johanson-Blizzard syndrome [[cite:PUB00094677]].

Name: E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase UBR2, UBR-box
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the UBR-box of human UBR2 and similar proteins found in vertebrates [[cite:PUB00103365]].

;

E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase UBR2 ([ec:2.3.2.27]), also called ubiquitin-protein ligase E3-alpha-II (E3alpha-II), or N-recognin-2, is a RING-type E3 ubiquitin ligase of the Arg/N-end rule degradation pathway. It recognises and binds to proteins bearing specific N-terminal residues that are destabilising according to the N-end rule, leading to their ubiquitination and subsequent degradation [[cite:PUB00103357], [cite:PUB00103353], [cite:PUB00058740], [cite:PUB00103358]]. UBR2 is associated with chromatin and controls chromatin dynamics and gene expression in both germ cells and somatic cells [[cite:PUB00103362], [cite:PUB00103364], [cite:PUB00103360]]. It plays an important role in spermatogenesis [[cite:PUB00103363], [cite:PUB00103359], , [cite:PUB00103361], [cite:PUB00044637], [cite:PUB00033697]].

Name: Nurim-like
ShortDescription:
Nurim is an inner nuclear membrane protein which may play an important role in the suppression of apoptosis [[cite:PUB00077048], [cite:PUB00077047]].

There are related enzymes in bacteria, including methanethiol S-methyltransferase ([ec:2.1.1.334]), which catalyses the methylation of methanethiol to yield dimethylsulphide (a volatile compound important in climate regulation) [[cite:PUB00089624]], suggesting a potential ancient origin [[cite:PUB00057231], [cite:PUB00079144]].

Name: Intraflagellar transport protein 20
ShortDescription: Intraflagellar transport (IFT) particle, which consists of complex A and B, is involved in assembling and maintaining eukaryotic cilia and flagella. Intraflagellar transport protein 20 (IFT20) is a subunit of the intraflagellar transport complex B (consists of IFT172, 88, 81, 80, 74/72, 57/55, 52, 46, 27, 20) [[cite:PUB00067617], [cite:PUB00067621]]. IFT20 is associated with the Golgi complex and may play a role in the trafficking of ciliary membrane proteins from the Golgi complex to the cilium [[cite:PUB00067619], [cite:PUB00067640]]. Besides its function in cilia, IFT20 also regulates immune synapse assembly in T cells [[cite:PUB00067639]]. In an yeast two hybrid experiment, IFT20 exhibited a strong interaction with IFT57/Hippi and the kinesin II subunit, KIF3B [[cite:PUB00067617]].

Name: Vitamin K epoxide reductase complex subunit 1
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the vitamin K epoxide reductase complex subunit VKORC1 and VKORC1L1 mostly from animals.

VKORC1 is an integral membrane protein that catalyzes the reduction of vitamin K 2,3-epoxide and vitamin K to vitamin K hydroquinone, an essential co-factor subsequently used in the γ-carboxylation of glutamic acid residues in blood coagulation enzymes [[cite:PUB00092943], [cite:PUB00016407]]. All homologues of VKOR contain an active site CXXC motif, which is switched between reduced and disulfide-bonded states during the reaction cycle [[cite:PUB00092945]]. Warfarin, a widely used oral anticoagulant used in medicine as well as rodenticides, inhibits the activity of VKOR, resulting in decreased levels of reduced vitamin K, which is required for the function of several clotting factors [[cite:PUB00057396]]. However, anticoagulation effect of warfarin is significantly associated with polymorphism of certain genes, including VKORC1. Interestingly, in rodents, an adaptive trait appears to have evolved convergently by selection on new or standing genetic polymorphisms in VKORC1 as well as by adaptive introgressive hybridization between species, likely brought about by human-mediated dispersal [[cite:PUB00092944]].

Name: Vitamin K epoxide reductase
ShortDescription: Vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR) recycles vitamin K 2,3-epoxide to vitamin K hydroquinone, a co-factor that is essential for the posttranslational γ-carboxylation of several blood coagulation factors [[cite:PUB00057396]]. VKORC1, the catalytic subunit of the VKOR complex, is a member of a large family of predicted enzymes that are present in vertebrates, Drosophila, plants, bacteria and archaea [[cite:PUB00016407], [cite:PUB00096863]]. Bacterial VKOR homologues catalyse disulphide bridge formation in secreted proteins by cooperating with a periplasmic, Trx-like redox partner [[cite:PUB00057392], [cite:PUB00057393]]. In fact, in some plant and bacterial homologues the VKORC1 homologous domain is fused with domains of the thioredoxin family of oxidoreductases [[cite:PUB00016407]]. VKOR is part of a disulphide bond formation pathway that uses electrons from cysteines of newly synthesized proteins to reduce a quinone [[cite:PUB00055212]].

Name: VKOR domain superfamily
ShortDescription: Vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR) recycles vitamin K 2,3-epoxide to vitamin K hydroquinone, a co-factor that is essential for the posttranslational γ-carboxylation of several blood coagulation factors [[cite:PUB00057396]]. VKORC1, the catalytic subunit of the VKOR complex, is a member of a large family of predicted enzymes that are present in vertebrates, Drosophila, plants, bacteria and archaea [[cite:PUB00016407], [cite:PUB00096863]]. Bacterial VKOR homologues catalyse disulphide bridge formation in secreted proteins by cooperating with a periplasmic, Trx-like redox partner [[cite:PUB00057392], [cite:PUB00057393]]. In fact, in some plant and bacterial homologues the VKORC1 homologous domain is fused with domains of the thioredoxin family of oxidoreductases [[cite:PUB00016407]]. VKOR is part of a disulphide bond formation pathway that uses electrons from cysteines of newly synthesized proteins to reduce a quinone [[cite:PUB00055212]].

Name: Zinc-finger C2H2-type 11
ShortDescription: This entry represents a zinc-finger of C2H2 type found in higher eukaryotes. It includes classical and closely related C2H2 or β-β-α zinc finger DNA-binding domains.

Name: ZNF592-like, C2H2 zinc finger
ShortDescription: This C2H2 zinc finger domain is found in a group of zinc-finger proteins such as ZN532, ZN687, ZN592 and related proteins which are probably involved in transcriptional regulation. A missense mutation in ZNF592 was found associated with CAMOS (Cerebellar Ataxia with Mental retardation, Optic atrophy and Skin abnormalities) syndrome [[cite:PUB00160211]].

Name: Zinc finger protein 532-like
ShortDescription: This entry represents Zinc finger protein 532 and related proteins from animals. Most members of this family contain several Zinc-finger C2H2-type domains. ZN532 is thought to be involved in transcriptional regulation.

Name: ATP12, ATP synthase F1-assembly protein, N-terminal
ShortDescription: This superfamily represents the N-terminal "wrist" domain of ATP12 ATPases which are required for the assembly of mitochondrial ATP synthase in all eukaryotes. The eukaryotic proteins include yeast Atp12 [[cite:PUB00014715]] and mammalian homologue ATPAF2 (ATP synthase mitochondrial F1 complex assembly factor 2) [[cite:PUB00081959]], which are required for assembly of the mitochondrial F1-ATPase.

Name: ATP12 orthogonal Bundle domain superfamily
ShortDescription: This superfamily represents an orthogonal bundle domain found in mitochondrial ATPase F1 complex assembly protein ATP12 [[cite:PUB00014715]] and homologue protein ATPAF2 (assembly factor 2) [[cite:PUB00054212]].

Name: ATP12, ATP synthase F1-assembly protein
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a group proteins from eukaryotes and bacteria that may have chaperone activity and be involved in F1 ATPase complex assembly. The eukaryotic proteins include yeast ATP12 [[cite:PUB00014715]] and mammalian homologue ATPAF2 (ATP synthase mitochondrial F1 complex assembly factor 2) [[cite:PUB00081959]], which are required for assembly of the mitochondrial F1-ATPase.

Mitochondrial F1-ATPase is an oligomeric enzyme composed of five distinct subunit polypeptides. The alpha and beta subunits make up the bulk of protein mass of F1. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae both subunits are synthesised as precursors with N-terminal targeting signals that are removed upon translocation of the proteins to the matrix compartment [[cite:PUB00014715]].

Name: Protein jagunal
ShortDescription: Protein jagunal is required for endoplasmic reticulum organisation and proper vesicular traffic during Drosophila oogenesis [[cite:PUB00068041]].

Name: Large ribosomal subunit protein mL50
ShortDescription: This entry represents the large ribosomal subunit protein mL50 from animals and fungi, previously known as L50 in humans [[cite:PUB00089007]] and L13 in yeast [[cite:PUB00089004], [cite:PUB00087081]].

Name: Stabilizer of axonemal microtubules 5
ShortDescription: This family (previously DUF4601) represents the homologs of Stabilizer of axonemal microtubules 5 (SAXO5, also known as C19orf45, TEX45). SAXO5 is a member of the SAXO superfamily of stabilizers that is ubiquitous in axonemal DMTs as well as stable microtubules of neurons and parasites. SAXO5 is a filamentous SAXO protein that binds along protofilament A04 with 96-nm periodicity [[cite:PUB00151496]]. A typical feature of SAXO proteins is the presence of Mn motif which forms a 5- to 6-residue helix flanked by a Tyr/Phe residue on one end and by a Ser/Thr on the other that binds the shoulder of the α-tubulin S9/S10 loop [[cite:PUB00151502]]. SAXO5 contains 11 Mn motifs and therefore has 96-nm periodicity, matching the external periodicity of the axoneme [[cite:PUB00151496]].

Name: RNA binding protein HABP4/SERBP1-like
ShortDescription:
This entry includes proteins with a hyaluronan/mRNA-binding protein domain, including HABP4 hyaluronan-binding proteins, PAI-RBP1 (also known as SERBP1) and related sequences.

HABP4 binds hyaluronan (a glucosaminoglycan), but according to its intracellular localisation, it may not be relevant in vivo. It has binds RNA and regulates transcription and pre-mRNA splicing [[cite:PUB00053771], [cite:PUB00053772], [cite:PUB00155126], [cite:PUB00076293], [cite:PUB00008623]].

SERBP1 is a ribosome-binding protein that promotes ribosome hibernation, a process during which ribosomes are stabilised in an inactive state and preserved from proteasomal degradation [[cite:PUB00155128]]. It acts via its association with EEF2/eEF2 factor, sequestering EEF2/eEF2 at the A-site of the ribosome and promoting ribosome stabilisation and storage in an inactive state and it may also play a role in the regulation of mRNA stability: binds to the 3'-most 134 nt of the SERPINE1/PAI1 mRNA, a region which confers cyclic nucleotide regulation of message decay [[cite:PUB00008624]]. It seems to play a role in PML-nuclear bodies formation [[cite:PUB00155127]]. The orthologue from S. pombe, oga-1, is a ribosome preservation factor that protects a small pool of nontranslating, vacant ribosomes in cells under nutrient starvation conditions. Under nutrient-limiting conditions, cells reduce ribosome biogenesis and degrade ribosomes via autophagy (ribophagy) or proteasomal degradation. It binds specifically G4 quadruplex (these are four-stranded right-handed helices, stabilised by guanine base quartets) and purine motif triplex (characterised by a third, antiparallel purine-rich DNA strand located within the major groove of a homopurine stretch of duplex DNA) nucleic acid structures. These structures may be present at telomeres or in rRNAs. Extends chronological lifespan when overexpressed [[cite:PUB00151550]].

Name: Intracellular hyaluronan-binding protein 4, N-terminal domain
ShortDescription: This is the N-terminal region of intracellular hyaluronan-binding protein 4 and SERPINE1 mRNA-binding protein 1-like proteins. This region carries nuclear localisation sites, and may also be involved in the binding to some of the partners in the translational machinery [[cite:PUB00008624], [cite:PUB00076292], [cite:PUB00076293]].

Name: Hyaluronan/mRNA-binding protein
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a domain found in the HABP4 protein family of hyaluronan-binding proteins, and the PAI-1 mRNA-binding protein, PAI-RBP1. HABP4 has been observed to bind hyaluronan (a glucosaminoglycan), but it is not known whether this is its primary rolein vivo. It has also been observed to bind RNA, but with a lower affinity than that for hyaluronan [[cite:PUB00008623]]. PAI-1 mRNA-binding protein specifically binds the mRNA of type-1 plasminogen activator inhibitor (PAI-1), and is thought to be involved in regulation of mRNA stability [[cite:PUB00008624]]. However, in both cases, the sequence motifs predicted to be important for ligand binding are not conserved throughout the family, so it is not known whether members of this family share a common function.

Hyaluronan/mRNA-binding protein may be involved in nuclear functions such as the remodeling of chromatin and the regulation of transcription [[cite:PUB00053771], [cite:PUB00053772]].

Name: Transmembrane protein 35A/B
ShortDescription:
Shedding of transmembrane protein 35 (TMEM35) produces a soluble peptide that may modulate neurite outgrowth in the adrenal zona glomerulosa after sodium depletion [[cite:PUB00056709]]. TMEM35 could be required for normal activity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and limbic circuitry [[cite:PUB00082567]].

TMEM35A, also known as NACHO, acts as a acetylcholine receptor chaperone that mediates the proper assembly and functional expression of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) throughout the brain [[cite:PUB00097836]].

Name: DoxX family
ShortDescription:
This is a family of integral membrane proteins known as DoxX, mostly from bacteria, archaea and animals. In M. tuberculosis, DoxX forms a membrane-associated oxidoreductase complex (MRC) together with the superoxide-detoxifying enzyme (SodA) and a predicted thiol-oxidoreductase (SseA) [[cite:PUB00101424]]. This complex physically links radical detoxification with cytosolic thiol homeostasis. All members of the MRC are required for the correct function as its impairments are correlated with defective recycling of mycothiol and accumulation of cellular oxidative damage [[cite:PUB00101424]].

This entry includes TMEM35A/B from animals. TMEM35A, also known as NACHO, acts as a acetylcholine receptor chaperone that mediates the proper assembly and functional expression of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) throughout the brain [[cite:PUB00097836]].

Name: WD repeat-containing protein 48
ShortDescription: The WDR48 family proteins are regulators of deubiquitinating complexes, enhancing the activity of USP1, USP12, and USP46 by increasing catalytic turnover without affecting substrate affinity. They play a crucial role in DNA repair processes, particularly by stimulating RAD51-mediated homologous recombination and participating in PCNA-mediated translesion synthesis. These proteins are also involved in the recruitment of RAD51 to replication forks under stress and bind both single-stranded and double-stranded DNA. In addition, they are implicated in cellular responses to viral infections, potentially affecting vesicular transport and membrane fusion events, as well as maintaining viral genomes. Some family members interact with ubiquitin and are involved in resistance to various compounds.

Name: WDR48/Bun107, ubiquitin-like domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents the ubiquitin-like domain of WDR48 from animals, Bun107 from fission yeasts and Duf1 from budding yeasts. WDR48 (also known as UAF1) is a regulator of deubiquitinating complexes [[cite:PUB00092494], [cite:PUB00092495], [cite:PUB00092496]]. Bun107 is required for the Ubp9 recruitment to septa and cell tips but also for its enzymatic activity at these specific locations [[cite:PUB00057398]].

Name: WD repeat creC family regulators
ShortDescription: The WD repeat creC family is involved in the regulation of carbon source utilization and protein stability through ubiquitination and deubiquitination processes. Members of the family function as components of a regulatory network that includes creA, creB, creC, creD, and acrB. They are essential for preventing the proteolysis of deubiquitinating enzymes such as CreB in the absence of carbon catabolite repression. By stabilizing CreB in a complex with CreC, they facilitate the expression of genes in specific metabolic pathways, including those for proline and quinate. Additionally, some family members act as regulators of deubiquitinating complexes, promoting the enzymatic activity of USP12 and other similar enzymes, and are involved in the localization and activity of deubiquitinating enzymes at specific cellular sites.

Name: Large ribosomal subunit protein uL30, bacteria
ShortDescription:
Ribosomal protein uL30 is one of the proteins from the large ribosomal subunit. uL30 belongs to a family of ribosomal proteins which, on the basis of sequence similarities, groups bacteria and archaea uL30, yeast mitochondrial uL33m, and Drosophila, slime mould, fungal and mammalian L7 ribosomal proteins [[cite:PUB00080279]]. uL30 from bacteria are small proteins of about 60 residues.

;

Ribosomes are the particles that catalyse mRNA-directed protein synthesis in all organisms. The codons of the mRNA are exposed on the ribosome to allow tRNA binding. This leads to the incorporation of amino acids into the growing polypeptide chain in accordance with the genetic information. Incoming amino acid monomers enter the ribosomal A site in the form of aminoacyl-tRNAs complexed with elongation factor Tu (EF-Tu) and GTP. The growing polypeptide chain, situated in the P site as peptidyl-tRNA, is then transferred to aminoacyl-tRNA, and the new peptidyl-tRNA, extended by one residue, is translocated to the P site with the aid of the elongation factor G (EF-G) and GTP as the deacylated tRNA is released from the ribosome through one or more exit sites [[cite:PUB00007068], [cite:PUB00007069]]. About 2/3 of the mass of the ribosome consists of RNA and 1/3 consists of protein. The proteins are named in accordance with the subunit of the ribosome which they belong to: the small (S1 to S31) and the large (L1 to L44). Usually they decorate the rRNA cores of the subunits.

Many ribosomal proteins, particularly those of the large subunit, are composed of a globular, surfaced-exposed domain with long finger-like projections that extend into the rRNA core to stabilise its structure. Most of the proteins interact with multiple RNA elements, often from different domains. In the large subunit, about 1/3 of the 23S rRNA nucleotides are at least in van der Waals' contact with protein, and L22 interacts with all six domains of the 23S rRNA. Proteins S4 and S7, which initiate assembly of the 16S rRNA, are located at junctions of five and four RNA helices, respectively. In this way, proteins serve to organise and stabilise the rRNA tertiary structure. While the crucial activities of decoding and peptide transfer are RNA-based, proteins play an active role in functions that may have evolved to streamline the process of protein synthesis. In addition to their function in the ribosome, many ribosomal proteins have some function 'outside' the ribosome [[cite:PUB00007069], [cite:PUB00007070]].

Name: Large ribosomal subunit protein uL30, ferredoxin-like fold domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
Ribosomal protein uL30 is one of the proteins from the large ribosomal subunit. uL30 belongs to a family of ribosomal proteins which, on the basis of sequence similarities [[cite:PUB00004400]], groups bacteria and archaea uL30, yeast mitochondrial L33, and Drosophila melanogaster, Dictyostelium discoideum (Slime mold), fungal and mammalian L7 ribosomal proteins which are now referred to as ul30m. uL30 from bacteria are small proteins of about 60 residues, those from archaea are proteins of about 150 residues, and eukaryotic L7 are proteins of about 250 to 270 residues.

This entry represents a domain superfamily with a ferredoxin-like fold, with a core structure consisting of core: β-α-β-α-β. This domain is found in prokaryotic ribosomal protein uL30 (short-chain member of the family), as well as in archaeal uL30 (L30a) (long-chain member of the family), the later containing an additional C-terminal (sub)domain).It is also found in nucleolar proteins with similarity to large ribosomal subunit L7 proteins. These are constituents of 66S pre-ribosomal particles and play an essential role in processing of precursors to the large ribosomal subunit RNAs [[cite:PUB00059243], [cite:PUB00059244], [cite:PUB00059245]].

Name: Large ribosomal subunit protein uL30-like, ferredoxin-like fold domain
ShortDescription:
Ribosomal protein uL30 is one of the proteins from the large ribosomal subunit. uL30 belongs to a family of ribosomal proteins which, on the basis of sequence similarities [[cite:PUB00004400]], groups bacteria and archaea uL30, yeast mitochondrial L33, and Drosophila melanogaster, Dictyostelium discoideum (Slime mold), fungal and mammalian L7 ribosomal proteins, also referred to as uL30m. uL30 from bacteria are small proteins of about 60 residues, those from archaea are proteins of about 150 residues, and eukaryotic L7 are proteins of about 250 to 270 residues. L30 is missing in some groups of bacteria, such as the CPR group, the PVC group, Cyanobacteria, and some symbionts, which suggests that it is non-essential [[cite:PUB00095413], [cite:PUB00095412]].

This entry represents a domain with a ferredoxin-like fold, with a core structure consisting of core: β-α-β-α-β. This domain is found in prokaryotic ribosomal protein uL30 (short-chain member of the family), as well as in archaeal uL30 (L30a) (long-chain member of the family), the later containing an additional C-terminal (sub)domain. It is also found in nucleolar proteins with similarity to large ribosomal subunit L7 proteins. These are constituents of 66S pre-ribosomal particles and play an essential role in processing of precursors to the large ribosomal subunit RNAs [[cite:PUB00059243], [cite:PUB00059244], [cite:PUB00059245]].

Name: DDX54/DBP10 family, DEAD-box helicase domain
ShortDescription:
This group of DEAD-box RNA helicases includes Dbp10 from fungi and DDX54 (also known as DP97) from mammals. DDX54 interacts in a hormone-dependent manner with nuclear receptors [[cite:PUB00101739], [cite:PUB00101740]]. It plays an important role in central nervous system myelination [[cite:PUB00078979]]. Dbp10 has a role in ribosome biogenesis [[cite:PUB00078980]].

;

This entry represents the DEAD-box helicase domain of DDX54 and similar eukaryotic proteins. This domain contains the ATP-binding region.

Name: DBP10, C-terminal
ShortDescription: This group of DEAD-box RNA helicases includes Dbp10 from fungi, DDX54 (also known as DP97) from mammals and RH29 from plants. DDX54 interacts in a hormone-dependent manner with nuclear receptors [[cite:PUB00101739], [cite:PUB00101740]]. It plays an important role in central nervous system myelination [[cite:PUB00078979]]. Dbp10 has a role in ribosome biogenesis [[cite:PUB00078980]]. RH29 is essential for the functional maturation of both male and female gametophytes [[cite:PUB00101741]].

Name: WD repeat protein DCAF11/LEC14B
ShortDescription: This entry includes a group of WD repeat proteins, including DDB1- and CUL4-associated factor 11 (DCAF11) from animals and LEC14B from plants. DCAF11 may function as a substrate receptor for CUL4-DDB1 E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase complex [[cite:PUB00041545]]. The function of LEC14B from plants is not clear.

Name: DDB1- and CUL4-associated factor
ShortDescription: This family of proteins appears to be involved in ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis, acting as potential substrate receptors for the CUL4-DDB1 E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase complex. Some members are implicated in the regulation of lifespan and neuronal degeneration in response to metal stress. They may also interact with the transcription factor SKN-1 to modulate gene expression.

Name: Cyclophilin-RNA interacting protein
ShortDescription: The name CRIP, for cyclophilin-RNA interacting protein, has been proposed for this family of proteins that comprise a cyclophilin-type peptidyl-prolyl isomerase domain, an RNA recognition motif, followed by a region rich in glutamate and lysine (EK domain) and a C-terminal string of serines [[cite:PUB00085560]]. The family includes among others Paramecium tetraurelia KIN241 [[cite:PUB00085560]], human cyclophilin-like protein PPIL4 [[cite:PUB00085564]], Arabidopsis thaliana AtCYP59 [[cite:PUB00085530]], and Caenorhabditis elegans sig-7 [[cite:PUB00085531]].

Name: Cyclophilin-like domain superfamily
ShortDescription: This superfamily represents a β-barrel domain that constitutes the core of cyclophilin-type peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerases ([interpro:IPR002130]) and can also be found in the C-terminal of some bacterial uncharacterised proteins, such as PH0987 from Pyrococcus horikoshii ([swissprot:O58715]) and [swissprot:Q81HJ5] from Bacillus cereus.

Name: PPIL4-like, cyclophilin domain
ShortDescription: This is a cyclophilin-type peptidylprolyl cis-trans isomerase domain occuring with a C-terminal RNA recognition motif domain (RRM). It is found in a number of eukaryotic cyclophilins having the RRM domain, including the nuclear proteins: human cyclophilin-like protein PPIL4 [[cite:PUB00085564]], Arabidopsis thaliana AtCYP59 [[cite:PUB00085530]], Caenorhabditis elegans sig-7 [[cite:PUB00085531]] and Paramecium tetrurelia Kin241. The Kin241 protein has been shown to have a role in cell morphogenesis [[cite:PUB00085560]].

Name: Cyclophilin-type peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase domain
ShortDescription:
Cyclophilins exhibit peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase (PPIase) activity ([ec:5.2.1.8]), accelerating protein folding by catalysing the cis-trans isomerisation of proline imidic peptide bonds in oligopeptides [[cite:PUB00017852], [cite:PUB00000320]]. They also have protein chaperone-like functions [[cite:PUB00021063]] and are the major high-affinity binding proteins for the immunosuppressive drug cyclosporin A (CSA) in vertebrates [[cite:PUB00017852]].

Cyclophilins are found in all prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and have been structurally conserved throughout evolution, implying their importance in cellular function [[cite:PUB00056846]]. They share a common 109 amino acid cyclophilin-like domain (CLD) and additional domains unique to each member of the family. The CLD domain contains the PPIase activity, while the unique domains are important for selection of protein substrates and subcellular compartmentalisation [[cite:PUB00056847]].
